_question: For one grammar and one set of wasm bytes, how far apart are the two tree-sitter runtimes this repo uses — and in which direction?
_why: Grammar patch G10 is ADMISSIBLE, fixes 7 corpus files under the CLI, and changes NOTHING in the product. The product loads the same wasm through web-tree-sitter 0.25.9; the CLI is 0.26.9. This measures the gap rather than leaving it as a story about one patch.
_method: Every tracked .ps1/.psm1 in powershell and ansible, parsed twice: once by web-tree-sitter 0.25.9 through the wired wasm (the product runtime), once by the tree-sitter CLI 0.26.9 (the tooling). Node LABELS are counted from each parse's own output, so a variable named $ERROR is not counted as an error node. Counts only — tree SHAPE is not compared, because a native-vs-wasm shape diff is exactly the comparison that misled G10.
conclusions: The disagreement is 9% of files and NOT one-directional: 41 files parse better under the tooling and 21 better under the product, so 'upgrade and everything improves' is not what the data says.

MISSING differs roughly five to one (107 product vs 20 tooling), which is a systematic difference in ERROR RECOVERY rather than in parsing — the runtimes agree on what is an error far more often than on what to insert to recover.

Therefore the CLI cannot validate a grammar patch's EFFECT. It can validate SAFETY — that no clean file changes shape — because a native-to-native tree diff compares one runtime with itself, which is how F11's G2 was pre-filtered. G10 is the counterexample for effect: 7 files 'fixed' natively, 0 in the product.
F11 (script/m14/verify-grammar-leaves.ts) is the only valid arbiter, because it runs on the product runtime. Its 'G1 fixed 0' row is not a weak signal to be explained away; it is the measurement.
This is not powershell-specific. Every lane loads its parser through the same web-tree-sitter 0.25.9, so any lane whose A/B work used the CLI has the same exposure.
